chapter_theme: Gunamalai's lovers' sulk is appeased and the two are joined in play, while the king's elephant, shamed since Civakan checked it, refuses food; the usurper Kattiyangaran, told the cause, sends his men to seize Civakan, who arms to fight but, recalling his teacher's word and at his foster parents' plea, lets himself be bound as the city wails and Sunandai falls in grief.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, raised by the merchant Kantukkatan
a merchant's daughter whom Civakan saved from the elephant and married
the minister who seized Saccandan's throne, the king of this chapter (வேந்தன், கொற்றவன்)
the king's war elephant that Civakan once checked when it charged Gunamalai
the mahout of the king's elephant
the swift young men the king sends to seize Civakan
the serving woman in Gunamalai's house who warns Civakan
the merchant who raised Civakan, his foster father (தாதை, தந்தை)

1070.reading: Gunamalai, in a lovers' sulk, tells Civakan that he came to praise the beauty of another woman's powder, that he has forgotten her and that the other dwells in his heart, and bids him go, asking whether she is a simple woman who cannot see it plainly.
1070.event: Gunamalai sulks and sends Civakan away, accusing him of thinking of another woman.
1070.nuance: The verse never names the woman of fine shoulders (நற்றோள் அவள்) or whose powder (சுண்ணம்) is meant; the powder recalls the scented-powder contest between Gunamalai and Suramanjari that began this ilampakam, and the charge may be a feigned one turned on his own praise. Who is meant cannot be fixed from this verse alone.

1071.reading: She leaves off her incense-scented silk, tears at her garland, rubs away the cool sandal, draws her bow-like brow tight, and with eyes like Kama's arrows reddening she sulks.
1071.event: Gunamalai strips off her ornaments and sulks with reddened eyes.
1071.nuance: Every act undoes an adornment: the sulk is shown as a woman unmaking the toilette made for love.

1072.reading: Civakan falls at the feet of the lightning-waisted woman and pleads, his words pour like water on the fire of her anger, the tears leave her eyes, and she looks at him with joy and heady pride.
1072.event: Civakan falls at Gunamalai's feet and pleads until her sulk gives way to joy.
1072.nuance: Line 2 is compressed (சொன்னீர் அவள் அழலுட் சொரிந்து ஆற்ற): his words are the water, her anger the fire, the image that the king's fire-like anger will answer a few verses later.

1073.reading: Civakan praises her as a golden creeper with soft shoulders like bamboo and young breasts under a gem ornament, saying that if the world were praised to its full worth it would only equal the price of her long bright eyes.

1074.reading: He clasps her in his arms, her coral lips and jewelled girdle gleaming, and desires the doll-like woman as nectar won on a lucky day.
1074.event: Civakan embraces Gunamalai and they are reconciled in love.

1075.reading: The narrator turns from the bright-faced, coral-mouthed woman of long painted eyes and her days of play with him to tell what befell the skilled one.
1075.nuance: A hinge verse: the play is cut off by வித்தகற்கு உற்றது, what came upon him, announcing trouble without naming it.

1076.reading: Ashamed since it fled from the prince that day, the elephant will not take its sugarcane and ghee-soaked balls of food, but stands sullen with its curved trunk hung between its moon-like tusks while bees hum about it.
1076.event: The king's elephant, shamed by its defeat by Civakan, refuses its food.
1076.nuance: The beast is given the lovers' own state: it stands with சுளிவு, sullen like a sulking woman, so the elephant's shame mirrors Gunamalai's ஊடல் in the verses just before.

1077.reading: Like a king whose enemy has turned his back, the king comes out in his earrings and sandal, his gold thread swaying on smoke-coloured silk, looks at the elephant standing in distress and asks what has come over it.
1077.event: The king sees his elephant off its food and asks what ails it.

1078.reading: Reading the king's mind, the mahout says he cannot tell for certain whether it is by the lord's grace or from great enmity, but that some days ago Civakan, to anger it, checked its must and this has made it so.
1078.event: The mahout tells the king that Civakan's checking of the elephant has broken its spirit.
1078.nuance: Lines 2 to 4 are hard: the mahout's hedge (நின் அருளினாம் கொல், செற்றம் மிக்குடைமையாற் கொல்) may be his own doubt or a sly hint that Civakan acted from enmity to the king; the mahout reads the king's குறிப்பு and words his report to feed it.

1079.reading: Twisting like a blazing fire-pit and glaring, the king, recalling that Civakan had beaten the troop of hill-chiefs in fierce battle, orders his men to seize at once and bring the merchant's son who planned a deed beneath his station, saying he will root out his strength.
1079.nuance: The elephant is only the occasion: the king remembers the earlier victory over the hill-raiders, so wounded pride over Civakan's rising fame drives the order. Calling him வாணிகன் மகன், the merchant's son, the usurper does not know whose son he has ordered taken. Lines 1 and 2 carry slips (நோககிக், கோக்குழர்ம்) and line 3 is obscure.

1080.reading: At the angry king's command the swift-footed young men run to kill and bring his life, wearing garlands of guts, smeared with blood and topped with fat like messengers of the lord of the south, Death, and reach the noble one.
1080.event: The king's men run to take Civakan and reach him.
1080.nuance: கொன்று உயிர் கொணர, 'kill and bring his life', is the king's order as the runners understand it; it exceeds the 'seize and bring' (பற்றுபு தம்மின்) of 1079, and the gore they wear makes them Death's envoys before any blow is struck.

1081.reading: Meanwhile he dresses her in a champak garland and sandal and camphor, draws with fragrant paste a love-creeper on her breasts that seems to climb to her face and put out tender leaves on her shoulders, and sets an ornament on her bright brow.
1081.nuance: The order of the verses sets the lovers' toilette directly against the runners' garlands of guts in 1080: two kinds of adornment, one of love and one of death, converge on the same house.

1082.reading: Civakan babbles the whole day to her: doll whose sweet speech the very melody bows to, where did you get the never-empty quiver of your dark eyes, from which you shoot without pause at me already wounded, foolish girl?
1082.nuance: பிதற்றினான், 'he babbled', is the narrator's word: the lover's talk is shown as delight that has lost its measure just as danger arrives.

1083.reading: While he of the golden anklet and his garlanded wife sat like the moon-crowned god and his consort, the king's men closed round like a pack of little jackals round a lion they despise, and the serving woman who saw it told the master.
1083.event: The king's men surround the house and the maid warns Civakan.

1084.reading: Hearing her, the hero of shoulders like twin saffron-smeared hills rose roaring like thunder and blazing like fire, like a maned lion coming out of its cave with its mate.
1084.event: Civakan rises in fury at the news.
1084.nuance: The lion of 1083, scorned by jackals, now comes out with its mate: the simile keeps Gunamalai at his side even as he turns to fight.

1085.reading: Holding up her flower-decked hair, gold-strand garland hanging, she cried 'what has happened to my lord of the garland?', and, unable to grasp more, stood shaking hard, like a great serpent struck by thunder in the rain.
1085.event: Gunamalai stands trembling in terror for Civakan.
1085.nuance: The four lines rhyme on மாலை in four senses (garland, the garlanded one, confusion, a garland-like serpent); the wordplay is the poet's, the terror hers.

1086.reading: Weighing the look of the hurrying men and the purpose they had in mind, he took up his killing bow so that it seemed to blaze, chose arrows fit to drink life, girded his garment tight, bound on his anklet and said 'tell me why you have come'.
1086.event: Civakan arms himself and demands the men's errand.

1087.reading: The men say that their king of command has graciously ordered that he come to the shade of his feet, and bid him of the fine-flower garland come; at this he flared up like thunder from the height of the sky and, burning like the god who shot the three fortified cities that would scorch the earth, spoke.
1087.event: The men deliver the summons and Civakan blazes in anger.
1087.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are the men's words inside the narration; அடிநிழல் தருக, come to the shade of the feet, is the courtesy of a summons to a subject, which the hero hears as a demand for submission.

1088.reading: Civakan says that after the king, desiring the breasts of a woman whose eyes outdo the sword, lost his hold, today may be the day this man's life slips and he falls, and bids a strong-armed companion harness the sturdy chariot.
1088.event: Civakan calls for his chariot to go against the king.
1088.nuance: Line 2 repeats words of 1087's line 2 (வருகென வானி னுச்சி) and is corrupt, so the sentence cannot be fixed. If the king of line 1 is Saccandan, who gave up rule for love of Vijayai, Civakan is naming his father's fall and the usurper's coming one; நந்த in line 3 may be a call to his brother Nandattan or a verb, 'to perish'.

1089.reading: The father of the sandal-chested hero reasons within himself that to contend with the king is the work of those bound to die, and that if they put off their burning anger, tie his hands and send him, the king's killing rage will cease; that is the wise course.
1089.event: Kantukkatan resolves to send Civakan bound to the king.

claims.claim: to set oneself against the king is the act of men who have come to their death

1089.nuance: Kantukkatan's prudence assumes the king's anger (அழற்சி) can be appeased by surrender; it echoes in reverse the teacher's demand in 393 that Civakan bear no அழற்சி against the usurper for a year. The merchant counsels submission to the man who killed Civakan's real father.

1090.reading: The hero of the bright spear, recalling his teacher's word, let his arms be bound behind him and stood with his anger quenched, while Sunandai and her husband said that going under the king's protection was the right course.
1090.event: Remembering his teacher's word, Civakan lets himself be bound.

claims.claim: to go under the king's protection is the virtuous course

1090.nuance: Two motives are given and kept apart: the parents' worldly counsel in line 4 and, decisively, the teacher's word (உவாத்தி சொல்) in line 1, the year's restraint promised in 393. Sunandai and Kantukkatan voice the claim together; voiced_by names him for both.

1091.reading: Because the mother who bore him and his father begged, saying this trouble had come, and bound him with the halter of the word that a noble one's manhood is not lessened by it, the mighty one, whose strength could crush the three worlds together and whose giving hand is like rain, was bound.
1091.event: At his foster parents' plea Civakan submits to being bound.

claims.claim: a noble man's manhood is not diminished by submitting at his parents' plea

1091.nuance: The verse calls Sunandai ஈன்றதாய், the mother who bore him, though she is his foster mother; it speaks as the household and the city know him. The real bond is the word (சொல் இமிழ்), not the cord. Line 2 (றோன்லுக் காண்மை) is corrupt, likely for தோன்றலுக்கு ஆண்மை.

1092.reading: As the warriors bound the twin shoulders of the long-haired prince with their belts, the old festive city wailed as if the serpent had seized the fiery god, the sun.
1092.event: The king's men bind Civakan's arms and the city laments.
1092.nuance: The eclipse simile makes the binding a cosmic and temporary darkening: the serpent swallows the sun only for a while, which forecasts his release.

1093.reading: Scattering the pearls on her shoulders, the pearls of her breasts and the pearls of tears streaming from her eyes, his foster mother cried 'my young one, Nambi, Civaka Sami!' and fell like lightning into the long sea of unending grief.
1093.event: Sunandai falls in grief as Civakan is led away.
1093.nuance: She calls him சீவக சாமி, 'lord Civaka', the name the invocation gives him, and the triple pearls (ornament, breast, tears) make one shower of loss.

links.note: In Kural 1316 the woman turns the man's 'I thought of you' into proof that he had forgotten her; in 1070 Gunamalai turns his praise of a powder into proof that he forgot her and keeps another in his heart (மறந்தீர், மனத்துள் உறைகின்றாள்).
links.teaches: The couplet's sulking logic, that any word of the lover proves his neglect, becomes in the epic a weapon aimed at a named rival's beauty, so feigned jealousy is how the epic's wife claims the hero among his many loves.

gains.a: the epic verse gains a recognised move of the ஊடல் convention that shows its accusation is play, not real suspicion
gains.b: the couplet gains a rival woman and a remembered contest as the occasion of the twisted word, which it leaves abstract

links.note: Kural 1109 names sulking, making up and union as love's rewards; verses 1071, 1072 and 1074 enact the three in order, sulk, appeasement at her feet, embrace.
links.teaches: The epic plays out the couplet's triad in full and then cuts it off with the king's runners, so love's three rewards are set as the calm the hero's karma-laden story breaks.

gains.a: the three verses gain a frame that makes them one completed movement rather than a string of descriptions
gains.b: the couplet gains a narrative cost: its rewards are shown as fragile, interrupted by a power outside the lovers

links.note: The patikam (14) tells how Civakan overcame the victorious elephant that frightened Gunamalai; in 1076 that same elephant, ashamed, refuses its food.
links.teaches: The victory the patikam lists as a rescue becomes, through the beast's shame and the mahout's report, the usurper's pretext for seizing the hero, so a deed of protection ripens into danger.

links.note: Kural 567 says harsh words and punishment past all bounds file down a king's conquering strength; in 1079 the king, raging over a sulking elephant, orders the hero seized and his strength rooted out.
links.teaches: The epic shows where such excess comes from: a usurper's envy of a subject's fame finds a trivial cause, and the order that follows is the first stroke of the file that will bring his own fall.

gains.a: the king's order gains a rule by which the reader can judge it as the self-wearing excess of a bad ruler, not just anger
gains.b: the couplet gains a source for excessive punishment in wounded pride, and a story in which the file's work can be traced

links.note: In the Silappathikaram the Pandya, inquiring into nothing, orders the guards to kill the thief and bring the anklet (கொன்றச் சிலம்பு கொணர்க); in 1080 the angry king's men run to kill and bring Civakan's life (கொன்றுயிர் கொணர) on a mahout's word.
links.teaches: The same unexamined order to kill and bring yields Kovalan's death and the bent sceptre in one epic but only a binding in the other, because Civakan chooses submission and a god he once helped intervenes; the Cintamani turns the scene of ripened evil into one where restraint and past kindness turn it aside.

links.note: Kural 895 says those who draw a mighty king's anger will survive nowhere; Kantukkatan reasons that to contend with the king is the work of the doomed (விளிகுற்றார்) and sends his son bound.
links.teaches: The merchant applies the couplet's prudence to a king who is a usurper and his son's true father's killer, showing that the rule of not provoking the strong counsels submission even to injustice, a cost the couplet does not weigh.

gains.a: Kantukkatan's choice gains the weight of received wisdom, so it reads as prudence rather than cowardice
gains.b: the couplet gains a case in which obeying it means yielding to an unjust king, which tests its scope

links.note: In 393 the teacher asks as his fee that Civakan bear no anger against the usurper for a year, and he agrees; in 1090, recalling his teacher's word, he lets his arms be bound with his anger quenched.
links.teaches: The vow made in private as a teacher's fee is what actually disarms the hero before the king's men, so the plot's turn depends on a kept promise rather than on the parents' prudence or the hero's weakness.

links.note: In 1092 the king's men bind Civakan's shoulders with their belts (கச்சின் வீக்கலின்); the patikam (16) tells how the god removed the flower-belt (பூங் கச்சு) that bound his shoulders.
links.teaches: The belt that binds the hero here is the very thing the patikam has the grateful god remove, so the eclipse simile's promise of a passing darkness is already answered at the epic's opening.

links.note: In 1090 Sunandai and her husband call going under the king's protection the right course; in 1093 she falls into a sea of unending grief as he is led away bound.
links.teaches: The foster mother who counselled submission as virtue cannot bear its result, so the chapter sets the household's prudent counsel against its cost to the one who gave it.

source_issues: 1071 line 1 prints தூமஞ் கமழ் where sandhi wants தூமங் கமழ்; a minor slip.
1079 line 1 prints நோககிக் for நோக்கிக், and line 2 கோக்குழர்ம் for கோக்குழாம் (TSCII slips).

1088 line 2 (கோளிழுக் குற்ற பின்றைக் வருகென வானி னுச்சி) repeats the words வருகென வானி னுச்சி of 1087 line 2 and breaks the second-letter rhyme in ளி of lines 1, 3 and 4; the line is corrupt, likely a copying error from the verse above.
1091 line 2 prints றோன்லுக் காண்மை, probably for (தோ)ன்றலுக் காண்மை with a letter lost.
1076 to 1091 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired).
